claim: NFPA 72 requires that at least 90 percent of measurement locations within each acoustically distinguishable space have a measured Speech Transmission Index of not less than 0.45 (0.65 CIS) and an average STI of not less than 0.50 (0.70 CIS) for mass-notification emergency communications.
source_title: Voice Intelligibility in Mass Notification Systems
supporting_excerpt: at least 90 percent of the measurement locations within each ADS have a measured Speech Transmission Index of not less than 0.45 (0.65 CIS) and an average STI of not less than 0.50 STI (0.70 CIS)
airport_or_entity: US mass notification systems generally; applies to certificated airports through NFPA adoption
units: STI dimensionless index; percent of measurement locations
denominator: measurement locations per acoustically distinguishable space
caveat: Secondary summary of NFPA 72; the primary code (NFPA 72 §18 / Annex D) is paywalled and should be cited directly in final packages.

claim: ACRP Research Report 175 states that codes and application standards typically recommend a minimum Speech Transmission Index of 0.45 or 0.50 for airport terminal PA intelligibility, with a target signal-to-noise ratio of 10 to 15 dB.
source_title: ACRP Research Report 175: Improving Intelligibility of Airport Terminal Public Address Systems — Chapter 3, Speech Intelligibility
supporting_excerpt: Codes and application standards typically recommend a minimum STI of 0.45 or 0.50 ... A good target for announcement levels is a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 10 to 15 dB.
denominator: per acoustically distinguishable space in terminal environment
caveat: ACRP guidance, not binding regulation; adoption is at the discretion of the airport authority.

claim: The 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design §219 require that in each assembly area where audible communication is integral to the space, an assistive listening system shall be provided, with receivers per Table 219.3 and at least 25% (minimum two) hearing-aid compatible.
source_title: ADA Standards for Assistive Listening Systems
supporting_excerpt: In each assembly area where audible communication is integral to the use of the space, an assistive listening system shall be provided ... Twenty-five percent minimum of receivers provided, but no fewer than two, shall be hearing-aid compatible.
airport_or_entity: US public accommodations including certificated airports subject to ADA Title II/III
caveat: Secondary summary; the primary text is the 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, §219 and §706, published by the US Access Board and DOJ.

claim: IEC 60268-16:2020, the international STI measurement standard, explicitly does not cover the case of fluctuating noise on the Speech Transmission Index.
source_title: IEC 60268-16:2020 — Sound system equipment, Part 16: Objective rating of speech intelligibility by speech transmission index
supporting_excerpt: The document does not cover the case of fluctuating noise on the STI, although some general comments on dealing with this complex issue are provided in 7.13 and 8.9.3.
airport_or_entity: Global measurement standard; relevant to any STI compliance regime for airport terminals
caveat: IEC 60268-16 is paywalled; scope language quoted from published summary of the standard's contents. Final citation should reference the standard directly.

claim: The SFO Quiet Airport program is reported in trade press to have removed over 90 minutes of unnecessary daily announcement time and reduced onsite noise by more than 40 percent, but no primary methodology (baseline dB, integration window, receiver locations, LEQ methodology) is published.
source_title: San Francisco Airport Removed 90 Minutes of Daily Noise — Travelers Say It Changed Everything
supporting_excerpt: removed over 90 minutes of unnecessary daily noise and achieved a reduction of more than 40 percent in overall onsite noise
units: minutes per day; percent noise reduction
caveat: Figures widely repeated but not accompanied by primary methodology; airport context packet flags the same gap.

claim: SFO's quiet-airport policy has been reported to increase risk of missed flights for passengers dining or shopping and to increase stress for passengers unfamiliar with the airport or language.
source_title: Why This Airport's 'Quiet Policy' Is Frustrating Some Passengers
supporting_excerpt: Passengers who choose to spend time shopping in duty-free stores or dining at airport restaurants are at an increased risk of missing their flights ... For many passengers, especially those unfamiliar with the local airport or language, the absence of announcements can be a significant source of stress.
caveat: Trade-press synthesis of passenger anecdotal reports; not a controlled passenger-experience study.

claim: London City Airport's silent terminal policy states that no tannoy announcements are made throughout the departure lounge, with customers relying on information screens for flight and gate information and PA reserved for emergencies.
source_title: Silent Terminal Policy at London City Airport
supporting_excerpt: No tannoy announcements are to be made throughout the departure lounge. Customers are to rely on information screens in order to obtain flight and gate announcements ... In the case of emergency are announcements made.
caveat: Secondary reporting of operator policy; LCY's own official page confirms silent-airport branding but the exhaustive operational protocol should be cited from LCY's primary documentation.

claim: London City Airport's noise management apparatus is oriented at aircraft departure noise and community-boundary compliance, not terminal-interior passenger acoustic experience.
source_title: London City Airport Noise Action Plan
supporting_excerpt: London City Airport runs a scheme of incentives and penalties based on departure noise levels, as measured by our noise monitoring system.
caveat: Confirms that LCY's noise regime is external/community-facing, not a terminal-acoustics analogue for MWAA's proposed standard.

claim: 14 CFR Part 139 requires each certificated airport to maintain an airport emergency plan and effective emergency communications procedures with sufficient detail to guide implementation.
source_title: 14 CFR Part 139 — Certification of Airports (FAR Part 139)
supporting_excerpt: Each certificated airport must maintain an effective communication system capable of alerting all emergency response personnel immediately when an aircraft incident or accident occurs; the airport emergency plan must contain sufficient detail to provide adequate guidance to each person who must implement these procedures.
airport_or_entity: All Part 139 certificated airports including IAD and DCA
caveat: Regulatory floor MWAA must satisfy regardless of any quiet-by-design overlay; any standard that reduces PA capability must preserve documented emergency reversion.

claim: MWAA plans approximately $5.5 billion of new debt between 2025 and 2028, with adjusted debt per O&D enplanement projected to peak near $400 in 2028 and net revenue debt service coverage expected to fall from 1.63x in 2024 to roughly 1.3x over the next five years.
source_title: Airport Context Packet — MWAA (IAD and DCA), §3 Financial position and debt capacity
supporting_excerpt: MWAA plans approximately $5.5 billion of new debt between 2025 and 2028. Adjusted debt per origin-and-destination enplanement is projected to peak near $400 in 2028 ... Net revenue debt service coverage is expected to fall from 1.63x in 2024 to roughly 1.3x over the next five years as new debt service phases in.
denominator: per O&D enplanement; debt-service coverage ratio
caveat: Context packet is Council-internal aggregation; final published cites should trace to Fitch, Moody's, S&P reports named in the packet.

claim: MWAA's 2020 seven-volume Design Manual is described by MWAA as a mandatory guide with the force of law on airport property, updated annually, with airport-specific supporting volumes for IAD and DCA.
source_title: Airport Context Packet — MWAA (IAD and DCA), §7 MWAA Design Manual and standards apparatus
page_or_section: §7 MWAA Design Manual and standards apparatus
supporting_excerpt: The Design Manual is described by MWAA as a mandatory guide with the force of law on the airport property, updated annually, with airport-specific supporting volumes for IAD and DCA.
caveat: Any quiet-by-design standard the Council recommends would be inserted through the Design Manual apparatus, not as a standalone policy.

claim: IAD's 2025 traffic mix was approximately 29.01 million passengers with 10.53 million international, or roughly 36%+ international share; DCA's was approximately 24.89 million passengers, down 5.4% year-over-year.
source_title: Airport Context Packet — MWAA (IAD and DCA), §6 Passenger and operational context
page_or_section: §6 Passenger and operational context (2025 calendar year)
supporting_excerpt: IAD: 29.01 million passengers, up 6.4% year-over-year; 10.53 million international passengers, roughly 36%+ international share ... DCA: 24.89 million passengers, down 5.4% year-over-year.
caveat: Context-packet aggregation; final citation should reference MWAA's traffic reporting or T-100 data.

claim: ACRP Research Report 239 provides assessment tools and notable practices for airport programs serving travelers with disabilities and older adults, addressing digital accessibility, facility accessibility, assistive services, communication, and wayfinding.
source_title: ACRP Research Report 239: Assessing Airport Programs for Travelers with Disabilities and Older Adults
supporting_excerpt: provides assessment tools and notable practices for airports to develop and evaluate programs, with practical suggestions related to digital accessibility (e.g., mobile apps) and facility accessibility, assistive services, communication, wayfinding, and ground transportation access issues.
caveat: Report treats digital/app channels as complements, not substitutes, for staffed and audio communication.

claim: Amsterdam Schiphol operates a silent-airport model in which important flight information is shown on Flight Information Display Systems and the app, with announcements limited to weather delays or genuine emergencies.
source_title: Silent Airports List 2026: The Global Guide to Quiet Terminals
supporting_excerpt: Schiphol describes itself as a Silent Airport with virtually no announcements, with important information shown exclusively on Flight Information Display Systems (FIDS) and the app. Announcements are made only for bad weather delays or genuine emergencies.
caveat: Trade-press aggregation of AMS operating description; primary source is Schiphol's own passenger information pages.
